newsitem.title: HUNGARY: TAX HIKES, FEWER CONFERENCES HIT DANUBIUS.
newsitem.headline: TAX HIKES, FEWER CONFERENCES HIT DANUBIUS.

text.p: Hotel group Danubius 's mixed first half results, with pre-tax profits up and the operating profit down, were mainly a result of higher taxes and fewer high-spending conference guests, the company said.

"Last year saw a lot of conferences as it was Hungary's 1100th anniversary and everyone focused on that," CEO Sandor Betegh told Reuters. "We have the same occupancy this year but not the same quality of guest."
Danubius's operating profit for January to June this year was 1.104 billion forints, compared to 1.663 billion forints in the first half of last year, the company reported on Monday.
Pre-tax profits rose to 2.524 billion from 1.813 billion in 1996 while net sales rose by less than inflation to 8.96 billion forints from 8.314 billion.
Inflation at the end of the first half of this year stood at 18.7 percent year on year.

Betegh said a fall in the proportion of conference guests had been expected and the final figures were better than expected. "If I consider everything the results are not bad -- the fall did not affect the figures as much as we expected."
Betegh said large increases in taxes, including the television tax, building and tourism taxes, had also eroded operating profits.
"The television tax was tripled and this alone cost us 50 million forints," he said.
Betegh said the relative weakness of the mark, with 60 percent of the company's guests coming from Germany, Austria and Switzerland, had also affected sales revenues.
One London-based analyst said on Monday that the forint is 10 percent overvalued against a generally weak German currency.
"The forint depreciation is in itself very important and this is influenced by the relatively weak mark," Betegh said.

The company's net financial income was boosted to 1.429 billion forints from 67 million forints in the first half of 1996 as a result of the handover by the state privatisation agency APV of 20 percent of the company's privatisation revenies under a 1992 law.
"We got back 1.4 billion forints," he said. "Of this 811 million went to the capital reserve with interest on it which is around 600 million."
Financial revenues were also boosted by profits from compensation coupons used to increase by 20 percent the company's stake in Hungarhotels, which Danubius acquired late last year, Betegh said.
On the Budapest Stock Exchange Danubius stocks had fallen 230 by 1020 GMT to 6,375.
